In adjudication, the APA contents itself with supplying procedural 
requirements for what administrative lawyers customarily call “formal 
hearings,” due to their similarity to civil trials. The APA’s formal hearing 
requirements may apply in either adjudication or in rulemaking, but only 
in limited circumstances that the statute identifies in two separate 
provisions that contain nearly identical language:
• 
In rulemaking: “When rules are required by statute to be 
made on the record after the opportunity for an agency 
hearing,” 5 U.S.C. § 553(c); and
• 
In adjudication: “In every case of adjudication required by 
statute to be determined on the record after opportunity for 
agency hearing,” id. § 554(a).
Thus, the APA provides minimum procedural requirements for a generic 
form of “on-the-record” hearing that must be used only when some other 
statute (typically the agency’s organic act) requires it. What uniformity 
might be provided by this approach has been undermined by confusion 
about the meaning of “on the record,” agency resistance to the use of formal 
hearings, and Congress’s tendency to displace the APA’s hearing provisions 
with unique hearing procedures designed to suit individual agency 
programs. Moreover, most adjudications are “informal,” in the sense that 
they are completed without a hearing. The APA does not specify minimum 
procedures for these informal adjudications. Each agency has broad 
discretion to fill in the procedural details of the informal, non-hearing 
adjudications contemplated by its organic act, which may include decisions 
on applications, investigations, inspections, examinations, negotiations, 
and settlements. The details often are found in procedural regulations that 
the agency has adopted and must follow.
Beyond statutory (and regulatory) requirements, constitutional due 
process has significant implications for administrative adjudication. As has 
already been suggested, the APA itself codified and built upon pre-APA due 
process law. And constitutional due process continues to serve as an 
independent check on agency action. Administrative processes, whether of 
federal or state origin, must provide affected parties with “due process.” 
But what process is due? That is a difficult and often-contested question. 
Here as elsewhere, in cases of doubt, courts fall back on what they perceive 
to be the legal system’s fundamental understandings and commitments. 
Indeed, much judicial “interpretation” of statutory hearing provisions 
might as easily be characterized as administrative common law. In 
addition, questions about due process typically are presented first to 
agencies and often are resolved without recourse to the courts. Due process 
is thus a core locus of administrative constitutionalism.
